title: HTML Challenge: Build a Real Page
description: Plan and build a complete HTML page combining headings, text, links, images, lists, a table, a form, and semantic elements into one coherent document.

objectives.statement: Plan the semantic structure of a complete HTML page from a requirements list before writing markup.
Combine headings, paragraphs, links, images, lists, a table, a form, and semantic elements into one coherent, correctly nested document.
Inspect a finished document for common structural, semantic, and accessibility mistakes, and explain the major structural decisions made.

content.title: HTML Challenge: Build a Real Page
content.hook: Every skill from this module so far has been isolated. Real pages need all of them at once, chosen correctly and combined into something coherent.
content.context: This is the first lesson where you decide the structure yourself, from a requirements list rather than a worked example.
goals: Plan a page's structure before writing markup
Combine every HTML skill from this module into one page
Find and explain your own structural decisions

content.title: Plan Before You Build
content.text: Before writing any markup for a real page, it helps to plan its semantic regions first: what's the header content, what's the main content, are there distinct articles or sections within it, is there a sidebar, what belongs in the footer? Once the regions are decided, the details — which parts are lists, which need a table, which need a form — follow naturally from what the content actually is, not from how you want it to look. This is the same planning habit professional developers use before writing a single line of a real feature.

callout.text: A fast planning technique: sketch just the semantic skeleton (header/nav/main/article-or-section/aside/footer) as comments first, then fill in the details inside each region.

content.keyTakeaway: Decide the semantic regions first; let the content's meaning decide the specific elements inside each region.

content.title: Build the Complete Page
content.prompt: Build a 'Local Hiking Club' page with: a header containing the club name; a nav with at least two links; a main containing an article introducing the club, a table of three upcoming hikes (date and location columns), an unordered list of three things to bring, and a labeled sign-up form (name and email, with a submit button); and a footer with a copyright line.
content.instructions: Use real semantic structure (header, nav, main, article, footer) rather than divs, a genuine table for the hikes, a genuine list for the checklist, and a properly labeled form.

content.title: Inspect a Similar Page for Mistakes
content.prompt: This similar hiking-club page has three planted mistakes: a heading level that skips from h1 to h3, a form label with no for attribute, and an image with a relative path that doesn't account for the file being one folder deeper than the images folder. Find and fix all three.
content.buggyCode:
Trail Runners Club

Weekly Meetups

We meet every Saturday.
content.bugDescription: Three separate structural mistakes: the article heading skips from h1 to h3 instead of h2; the label has no for attribute matching the input's id; and the image path 'images/trail.jpg' resolves relative to /site/pages/, not to /site/, so it needs to go up one level.
fixRequirements: Article heading should be h2, not h3
Label needs for="email" to match the input's id
Image src should correctly resolve to /site/images/trail.jpg from /site/pages/about.html

feedback.correct: All three structural mistakes found and fixed.
feedback.incorrect: Check all three: the heading level, the label association, and the image path — there are three separate mistakes to find.

content.prompt: Explain the major structural decisions you made while building your hiking club page: why you chose the semantic regions you did, why the hikes belonged in a table rather than a list, and why the checklist belonged in a list rather than a table.
guidelines: Focus on why each choice matched the content's actual meaning, not just that it worked.

content.title: What You Should Take Away
takeaways: Planning a page's semantic regions before writing markup makes the rest of the structure follow naturally.
A real page combines headings, text, links, images, lists, tables, and forms, chosen based on what each part of the content actually is.
Reviewing a finished page for structural and accessibility mistakes is itself a skill worth practicing deliberately.
